name: Pennine Way
description: Steeped in history and traversing spectacular landscapes, the iconic Pennine Way stretches for 268 miles (431 km) across England’s wild northern uplands. The route follows England’s rocky spine from the hills of the Derbyshire Peak District and the Yorkshire Dales, through the stunning Swaledale Valley, across the North Pennines and over Hadrian’s Wall in Northumberland to the Cheviot Hills, ending in the Scottish Borders in Kirk Yetholm.

name: Whitefield Moor, Hampshire
description: This walk includes some of the most interesting features of the New Forest. The route takes in part of Ober Water and all of the Tall Trees Trail lining the Rhinefield Drive with its amazing redwoods and firs planted in 1859. As you return to the start, you may spot shaggy Highland cattle around the pools and streams. By Dorothy Hamilton

name: Offa's Dyke Path
description: Following the spectacular dyke King Offa ordered to be constructed in the 8th century Offa’s Dyke Path provides 177 miles (285 Km) of stunning walking. Starting at Sedbury Cliffs near Chepstow on the banks of the Severn estuary it runs along the English Welsh border to reach the coastal town of Prestatyn on the shores of the Irish sea. Following valleys and rocky ridges the walk is ever changing but always fascinating.

name: South Downs Way
description: The 100 mile (160 Km) long South Downs Way follows the old routes and droveways along the chalk escarpment and ridges of the South Downs. Enjoy the stunning long distance views, picturesque villages, thatched pubs and cosy tea rooms.

name: The Ridgeway
description: The Ridgeway, Britain’s oldest road, follows the same route over the high ground used since prehistoric times by travellers, herdsmen and soldiers. Travel on a journey through time for 87 miles (139 Km). Experience wide, open views of rolling chalk downland and explore the many archaeological treasures close to the Trail including Neolithic long barrows, Bronze Age round barrows, Iron Age forts and the figures of white horses cut into the chalk. Relax in the evening at a cosy pub in one of the villages or small towns along the trail.

name: North Downs Way
description: The North Downs Way National Trail is 153 mile trail through coast and countryside, with easy access from London. Walk or cycle across stunning chalk escarpments, pass through the Surrey Hills and Kent Downs Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty, and over wooded hills and magnificent valleys.

name: Yorkshire Wolds Way
description: The Yorkshire Wolds Way wends for 79 mile (127 km) through some of the most tranquil and gentle countryside in England. From the banks of the mighty Humber estuary, along wooded slopes and through serene dry valleys, the walk climbs gently onto the airy tops of the rolling hills where on a clear day "you can see forever". With vineyards, lavender farms and Buddhist centres as well as cosy welcoming pubs it’s a trail of surprises.

name: Peddars Way and Norfolk Coast Path
description: Whether it’s the deep history of early man, the medieval ports and churches of the north coast, big-sky views or the culinary adventures made possible by some of the country’s finest pubs and local producers, there’s something for everyone along the Peddars Way and Norfolk Coast Path National Trail.

name: Thames Path
description: Following England's best known river for 185 as it meanders from its source in the Cotswolds through several rural counties and on into the heart of London. Enjoy peaceful water meadows rich in wildlife, historic towns and cities and many lovely villages, finishing at Woolwich just a few miles from the sea.

name: Hadrian's Wall Path
description: Following the historic UNESCO World Heritage Site of Hadrian’s Wall from coast to coast, the Hadrian’s Wall Path National Trail is an 84-mile (135 km) pathway passing through a diverse landscape where magnificent moorland gives way to rolling fields and there are dozens of sights to behold.

name: Cotswold Way
description: With over 102 miles (164km) of magical walking, magnificent views, ancient sites and beautiful villages, the Cotswold Way offers a taste of the South you won’t forget. The route offers a quintessentially English experience through flower-filled meadows, wonderful beech woodland, charming towns and villages and past historic sites – with amazing views from the Cotswold escarpment.

name: Pennine Bridleway
description: A 10 mile circuit, the Settle Loop is part of the Pennine Bridleway National Trail.  This route starts and finishes in Settle and passes through the wonderful limestone uplands of the Yorkshire Dales National Park, with spectacular views across Malham Tarn.  Settle is on the iconic Settle to Carlisle Railway line and is a working town with a popular market and a good range of independent shops and plenty of places to eat and drink.  It is recommended to walk the route anti-clockwise to avoid a steep climb out of Settle at the start of the route, but it can be enjoyed in either direction.

name: Cleveland Way
description: The 109 mile (175km) Cleveland Way is one of England’s original National Trails. Starting at Helmsley, the first half crosses the North York Moors National Park, boasting great vistas from sweeping heather moorlands. Upon reaching the coast at Saltburn-by-the-Sea, the second half of the route then follows the North Yorkshire coast as far as Filey, taking in the highest cliffs in eastern England at Boulby.

name: South West Coast Path
description: The South West Coast Path is a 630 mile (1,014 km) journey along the coastline of England’s southwest peninsula. Running from Minehead in Somerset to Poole in Dorset, the longest of England’s National Trails has a wealth of stunning natural scenery, sea views, pretty ports and historic county towns. The Path has won numerous awards and offers a truly unique experience: this is walking at its most challenging and most rewarding.

name: Jacobs ladder
description: Jacob's Ladder on Pen y Fan is a notoriously steep, kilometer-long, stone-stepped path located on the southeast side of the mountain, leading down towards Cribyn. Known for being a "leg-breaker" in the Fan Dance special forces challenge, it is a popular but challenging, strenuous ascent or descent that offers dramatic, scenic views of the Brecon Beacons

name: Cadair Idris (Minffordd Path), Gwynedd
description: This is one of the great British mountain walks, starting in thick oak woodland and rising to the immense rocky amphitheatre that surrounds the hidden lake of Lyn Cau. The approach to Cadair's true high point traverses a broad rocky ridgeline, climbs to a perfect pyramidal summit, then drops again before leading upwards through an ancient volcanic landscape to the trig point and shelter at Penygadair. From the 893m summit you're treated to magical views across the surrounding peaks and lakes, out to the west coast, and north to the Llyn Peninsula and the distant mountains of northern Snowdonia. This is a rocky and steep route on good paths, but requires care and navigation skills in low visibility. Go prepared for all weathers, with good outdoor gear and plenty of refreshments, and you'll come back telling tales of soaring peaks forged by mythical giants, crowned by rocks that are older than the dinosaurs.

name: Fairfield Horseshoe
description: Fairfield Horseshoe is a classic circular hillwalking ridge walk route starting from Rydal or Ambleside in the English Lake District that takes in all the fells that surround the valley of the Rydal Beck. The walk is extremely popular and follows well defined paths throughout with no real difficulties; however, care should be taken on the summit of Fairfield in poor visibility as the plateau of that mountain is very flat and can be quite confusing, with the danger of steep drops to the north and west. The eastern side of the horseshoe from Low Sweden Bridge near Ambleside to the slopes of Hart Crag follows a high dry stone wall, covering some six kilometres, making navigation simple even in poor weather conditions.

name: Ben Nevis
description: Ben Nevis is the highest mountain in Britain and it makes you work for every one of those 4411ft. It's a long, relentless climb from Achintee to Red Burn, and then up the zig-zags to the summit (and you have to come down the same way). But wait until at least May to climb it; in winter conditions it's for mountaineers only. By Nick Hallissey

name: Lake District, Grasmere
description: This walk forms part of Ordnance Survey's 'Short Walks Made Easy' series, which offer leisurely walks between 1 and 5 miles, with simple to follow step-by-step instructions; essential logistical information including accessibility, parking & dog suitability; fascinating local information and nature guides; and stunning photography.

name: Falls of Foyers
description: The Upper and Lower Falls of Foyers are located above Loch Ness and Foyers Bay, and make the basis for a great walking circuit for active families. This route starts above the falls (where you will find a cafe, carpark and toilets) and descends past the impressive Lower Falls to pass a wild gorge and reach Lower Foyers. The return route is up good forest tracks, to pass the Upper Falls. After this, a quiet road takes you back to the start. There are some steep ascents and descents in places. By Steve Goodier

name: Bath Skyline
description: Bath is perfectly designed for panoramic cityscapes. It is built from honey-golden limestone and surrounded by hills, from which the city can show off its Regency crescents and Gothic abbey. The National Trust's free, well-waymarked Skyline Walk winds through woods and fields above the eastern edge of the city, passing splendid views. By Phoebe Taplin

name: Four Waterfalls Walk
description: The sublime nature of waterfalls have always held a thunderous appeal for lovers of the wild. The evocative names given to the 'four waterfalls' in Waterfall Country include Sgwd Clun-Gwyn (Fall of the White Meadow) and Sgwd yr Eira (Fall of Snow). They form part of the rivers Mellte and Hepste.

name: Luds Church and the Roaches
description: The jagged ridge of the Roaches is one of the most popular outdoor locations in the Peak District National Park. The name is a corruption of the French for rocks - roches. It was here on the gritstone crags that the ‘working class revolution’ in climbing took place in the 1950s. Manchester lads, Joe Brown, a builder, and Don Whillans, a plumber, went on to become legends within the climbing fraternity by developing new rock climbing techniques wearing gym shoes and using Joe’s mother’s discarded clothes line as a rope. Other, less tangible legends, surround this long outcrop, several of them attached to Doxey Pool. Locals speak in hushed voices of a young mermaid, who lived in the pool but was captured by a group of men. If the stories are to be believed her ghost can still be heard singing through the mist. Lurking in the darkest depths of the pool is Jenny Greenteeth, a hideous monster with green skin, long hair and sharp teeth, who grabs the ankles of anyone unfortunate enough to get too close, dragging them to a watery grave.Sir gawain and the Green Knight: But the greatest legend associated with the Roaches is the Arthurian tale of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. According to the 14th-century poem a knight on horseback, cloaked entirely in green, gatecrashed a feast at Camelot and challenged the Knights of the Round Table. Sir Gawain rose to the challenge and beheaded the Green Knight but the latter retrieved his head and laughingly challenged Sir Gawain to meet with him again, in a year’s time, at the Green Chapel. This has been identified as Lud’s Church, near the Roaches. In the 1950s Professor Ralph Elliot, now of the University of Adelaide in Australia, identified the Roaches as the general location of the chapel from the text. Great crooked crags, cruelly jagged, the bristling barbs of rock seemed to brush the sky Professor Elliot’s theory was supported by a group of linguists, working on the poem at the same time, who placed the work in the same 15-mile (25km) radius. The professor and a group of students from Keele University, where he was then based, tramped all over the countryside looking for a suitable cave to match the poetic description. A hole in each end and on either side, And overgrown with grass and great patches All hollow it was within, only an old cavern Or the crevice of an ancient crag Lud’s Church fitted the bill. This rocky cleft was created by a mass of sandstone slipping away from the slope of the hill. It was here that Sir Gawain kept his rendezvous with the Green Knight resulting in that ghostly gentleman losing his head for a second time.While you're there: Leek is a magnet for antique hunters. As well as having a host of antique dealers, there’s an open-air craft and antique market each Saturday in the historic Market Square. Other markets include the Butter Market, selling mainly fresh traditional produce, on Wednesday, Friday and Saturday. Also worth visiting is the water-powered corn mill at Brindley’s Mill.Where to eat and drink: The Roaches Tearoom at Paddock Farm sits beneath the rocky outcrop of Hen’s Cloud almost opposite the car parking area. The food is home-made, excellent and there’s plenty of it. There’s a conservatory overlooking a herb garden and superb views across Tittesworth Reservoir. It’s open daily all year.

name: Balmoral Cairns, Aberdeenshire
description: Cairns are man-made mounds of stone. Some mark high points and others mark trails. But on the Balmoral Estate in the southeast quarter of the Cairngorms National Park, there are 11 cairns more elaborate than any others you'll find in Britain. Built for royalty, the Balmoral cairns mark important events in the lives of Queen Victoria and her family, who bought Balmoral Castle in 1852. It remains a favourite residence of the current queen. Building the cairns was a family affair, with each member of Victoria's large family and entourage placing stones. Most celebrate her children's marriages, but the largest – a huge pyramid erected in 1862 – commemorates the passing of her beloved husband Prince Albert. This walk explores forest trails linking eight of the cairns, including the oldest and grandest. Through breaks in the clustered ranks of Scots pine, you're treated to sweeping views over Deeside and the castle, and a window on the majestic lines of Lochnagar. Rising to 3789 feet, this mountain easily earns its status as a Munro. By Philip Thomas

name: The Northern Trek 8. Horton in Ribblesdale to Hawes
description:
Horton in Ribblesdale is the starting point of Yorkshire’s most famous walk - The Three Peaks (Pen-Y-Ghent, Whernside and Ingleborough). It’s a tough walk of 24 miles and has to be completed in 12 hours. Every weekend in summer hundreds of people will walk it. It is a true right of passage for many Yorkshire folk, and will always be one of my favourite walks. It's a walk worth coming back for. You will undoubtably meet 'Three Peakers' whilst in Horton.
 
However, The Northern Trek continues to follow The Pennine Way over the tops to Wensleydale. The paved path out of Horton is worth noting - it is the front cover photograph of Alfred Wainwrights famous book on The Pennine Way

name: The Great Glen Way, Scottish Highlands
description: The Great Glen Way long-distance trail runs for 73 miles from coast-to-coast across the Scottish Highlands, linking the towns of Fort William and Inverness.

name: Glencoe Lochan Trail
description: A gentle trail around the tranquil Glencoe Lochan and woodland, created by Lord Strathcona for his homesick Canadian wife. A wide, firm and smooth surfaced path, generally flat, but with short gentle gradients, broken up with rest points.  At the far end of the Lochan during times of high rainfall a section of the path up to 3 meters long may be covered in surface water.

name: Loch Achtriochtan
description: Loch Achtriochtan or Loch Trychardan is a small shallow freshwater loch located to the east of Glencoe village in Lochaber in the Scottish Highlands. It is now under the care of the National Trust for Scotland.

name: Conic Hill, Stirlingshire
description: Conic Hill is a popular 361-meter hill in Balmaha, Scotland, offering panoramic views of Loch Lomond and its islands. Located on the Highland Boundary Fault, it is a renowned, easily accessible, and family-friendly section of the West Highland Way. The hike typically takes 1.5–3 hours to complete.

name: Cat Bells, Cumbria
description: From the moment you step on the fell you can start to enjoy sensational panoramic views over Keswick, Derwent Water and Borrowdale. Add to this to the West the views of Newlands Valley and the Western Fells making this walk unrivalled in spectacular views.

name: Scafell Pike, Cumbria
description: Scafell Pike is England's highest, and perhaps most iconic, mountain. But standing atop its towering summit is not simply about bagging the country's loftiest peak. Scafell Pike is also the nation's greatest war memorial; a place of beauty and grandeur to pay tribute to fallen heroes. In 1919, the mountain was bequeathed to the nation in 'perpetual memory of the men...who fell for God and King, for freedom, peace and right in the Great War'. So, when you're hiking this gloriously rugged and airy route up Scafell Pike from Borrowdale, spend a quiet moment to think of those men - after all, you're enjoying the freedom they fought for. By James Forrest

name: Snowdon – Pyg Track & Miners' Track
description: A classic ascent of Snowdon, starting from Pen-y-Pass and heading up the Pyg Track to the summit. You return via the Miners' Track, passing directly the stunning mountain lakes of Glaslyn and Llyn Llydaw.

name: Snowdon - Llanberis Path
description:
The Llanberis Path is undoubtedly the most popular in the National Park. Over 600,000 people reach the summit of Yr Wyddfa each year, and most walkers take the Llanberis Path to the peak.

 As one of the six main routes to the summit of Yr Wyddfa, the Llanberis path is a popular choice for those who are climbing Yr Wyddfa for the first time. While it’s the longest route, it does offer the most gradual climb to the peak. 

 While the Llanberis Path is often described as the ‘easiest route to the summit’, you should never underestimate any of the routes to the peak of Yr Wyddfa. Reaching the summit of Yr Wyddfa is a challenging undertaking. The  National Park Authority classifies Llanberis Path as a hard and strenuous route. A good level of fitness is required and navigation skills are essential.

name: Pen y Fan
description: The mountains of the Brecon Beacons National Park were made for ‘big high, little effort’ walking. They offer an almost infinite count of long, level grassy ridges that tower above deeply cloven cwms, offering fine views and providing easy access to the summits. Each massif has its own classic route, but the pick of the bunch must be the ascent of the ‘big three’ – Pen y Fan, Corn Du and Cribyn – from the beautiful Neuadd Reservoirs. This is a skyline walk par excellence, starting at a very respectable 440m and gaining the main southern ridge of Corn Du with only 200m of steep stuff to contend with. The next 4km is high-level hill-walking heaven as the ridge curls around the edge of the shapely Taf Fechan valley, gaining its height so gradually that you barely notice it. At the same time you get wonderful views in all directions, particularly at the halfway stage, when a slender, airy walkway known as Rhiw yr Ysgyfarnog (the ridge of the hare) provides a steep-sided head wall for Cwm Crew. Bwlch Duwynt marks the finish line for this one, and the starting post for the two tallest peaks in southern Britain. But the work’s all done now and it’s an easy task to gain both, with just the smallest amount of reascent separating the pair. There is a sting in the tail, though. It’s over 200m down from Pen y Fan into its eastern col, and this leaves you 130m short of Cribyn’s compact top. Have you the energy for one more climb? If not, there’s an easy get-out – a well-trodden escape path that flanks the mountain to the south

name: Dragon's Back
description:
This is a fantastic route if you have children who are obsessed with the mythical fire-breathing, barbed-tailed reptiles from their favourite stories. Granted, if you sell it to them like that, they might be a little underwhelmed on this walk, but the Dragon’s Back is still a sight to behold, so named because the undulating hills and ridges resemble a sleeping dragon.

 Along this walk, you’ll climb Waun Fach which is the highest point in the Black Mountains and also the second-highest mountain in the south of Britain with a summit height of 811 metres. Wild ponies roam and livestock graze in amongst the hills so keep your eyes peeled for this as you meander along the ups and downs on the spine of this sleeping giant. You may spot Castell Dinas hill fort along the way too, the highest castle in England and Wales, standing at 450 metres. Although a little harsher on the legs, it’s worth keeping to the peaks of the ridges as the 360-degree views are out of this world.

name: Waun Fach, Powys
description: This excellent horseshoe route encircles the head of the Rhiangoll valley, taking in the highest castle in Wales, the Y Grib ridge (also known as the Dragon's Back), considered the finest ridge in the area, and the highest point of the Black Mountains, Waun Fach (810m), not a peak as such, but a large flat top. Thanks to repairs to Waun Fach paths (used in this walk) in recent years, the walking is a lot easier and more pleasant than in the past. By Fiona Barltrop

name: Cheddar Gorge, Somerset
description: Somerset’s answer to the Grand Canyon, Cheddar Gorge began life 1.2 million years ago. How’s that for extra mature? During cold periglacial periods, meltwater abraded the Carboniferous Limestone of the Mendip Hills, gradually scooping out the rocky chasm we see today. Admittedly not quite so wide, deep or long as its Arizonan lookalike, with its river now flowing underground, it’s eye-popping all the same; nowhere more so than from its vertiginous rim, traversed by the Gorge Walk trail. Short but stirring, it’s easily the most sensational 3¾-mile loop in the district. But it’s not all about bumper views across the Somerset Levels. There are crag-hopping feral goats and hurtling peregrine falcons to spot. And from spring through to late summer, lime-loving wildflowers spangle the gorge, among them the rare little robin and Somerset’s county flower, the Cheddar Pink.

name: Tolkien Trail (Ribble Valley)
description: The Tolkien Trail in the Ribble Valley is a scenic circular walk in Lancashire, England, closely associated with the famous author J. R. R. Tolkien. The route passes through charming countryside, including the village of Hurst Green, the grounds of Stonyhurst College, and along the peaceful River Ribble. It is believed that Tolkien found inspiration here while staying at the college, with the landscape influencing elements of his work, particularly The Lord of the Rings. The trail offers a mix of woodland paths, open fields, and riverside views, making it a popular and accessible walk for both literature enthusiasts and nature lovers.

name: Bleaklow
description: Bleaklow in Derbyshire is a vast and atmospheric moorland plateau located in the Peak District, known for its wild, rugged beauty and remote feel. Characterised by peat bogs, heather, and gritstone formations, it offers a more challenging hiking experience compared to other areas in the national park. The area is also home to the wreckage site of a Bleaklow Bomber Crash, which has become a notable landmark for walkers. With sweeping views and a sense of isolation, Bleaklow appeals to experienced hikers seeking a dramatic and less crowded landscape.

name: Golden Cap
description: Golden Cap in Dorset is the highest point on the south coast of England, offering striking views across the Jurassic Coast and the English Channel. Located within Jurassic Coast, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the hill is known for its distinctive golden sandstone cliffs and rich geological history. The walk to the summit can be steep but rewarding, with paths passing through rolling countryside and coastal scenery. Popular with walkers and nature enthusiasts, Golden Cap provides a memorable combination of dramatic landscapes and panoramic coastal vistas.

name: Studland & Old Harry Rock
description: Studland and Old Harry Rocks in Dorset offer a striking coastal walk combining sandy beaches, heathland, and dramatic chalk formations. Located along the Jurassic Coast, this area is famous for the iconic white stacks of Old Harry Rocks, which rise sharply from the sea. The route typically passes through Studland Bay, known for its sweeping shoreline and diverse wildlife habitats. With relatively gentle terrain and stunning sea views, it’s a popular choice for a relaxed yet visually impressive coastal walk.

name: Lyme Regis
description: Lyme Regis, located on the Dorset–Devon border, is a charming coastal town known for its fossil-rich cliffs and historic seaside character. Part of the Jurassic Coast, it has long attracted visitors interested in geology and natural history, famously associated with fossil hunter Mary Anning. The area offers scenic coastal walks, including routes along the Cobb harbour and surrounding cliffs, with sweeping views of the English Channel. Combining picturesque streets, beaches, and scientific significance, Lyme Regis is a popular destination for both walkers and history enthusiasts.

name: Corfe Castle
description: Corfe Castle in Dorset is a historic village dominated by the dramatic ruins of Corfe Castle, a medieval fortress built by William the Conqueror. Set within the rolling Purbeck Hills, the area offers scenic walking routes through countryside, woodland, and along parts of the Purbeck Ridge. The castle played a significant role in English history, particularly during the English Civil War, when it was partially destroyed. Today, it’s a popular spot for walkers and history enthusiasts, combining striking views, rich heritage, and a picturesque village setting.
